title: Review: Strong and weak acids; Titrations and solution calculations; Indicators
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB03#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB03#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB08#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB03#N.3a, AB08#N.3a, AM08#N.13, AM08b#N.5, AB03#N.4a, AB08#N.10a, AM08#N.6a, AM08b#N.3, AB03#N.11, AB08#N.8, AM08#N.9, AM08b#N.10. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Concentration
items.clue: The amount of a dissolved substance per unit volume.

items.label: Strong acid
items.clue: Dissociates effectively completely in water, as HNO₃ does.

items.label: End point
items.clue: The stage of a titration at which the indicator visibly changes.

items.label: Phenolphthalein
items.clue: A weak acid, HInd, whose Ind⁻ form is pink; it changes at about pH 8–10.

questions.stem: A solution of nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), has a concentration of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Which statement about this solution is correct?

options.text: It is a weak acid, as its concentration is low.
It contains mainly HNO₃ molecules with a few ions.
It is a dilute solution of an acid that is fully dissociated.
It is neutral, as this much water neutralises the acid.

questions.explanation: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ completely, so [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Strength and concentration are independent.

questions.stem: An indicator, HInd, has pKa = 3.7: HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq). HInd is red and Ind⁻ is yellow. What colour does the indicator show in a solution of pH 6.0, and why?

options.text: Yellow, as Ind⁻ predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Red, as the solution is acidic, with its pH below 7.
Red, as HInd predominates when the pH is above the pKa.
Orange, as HInd and Ind⁻ are equal at equilibrium.

questions.explanation: At pH 6.0, [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁶ mol dm⁻³, far below Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁴, so the equilibrium lies to the right: [Ind⁻]/[HInd] ≈ 200. The colour is yellow.

questions.stem: A student titrates 25.0 cm³ of a weak acid, HA, with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. The student then titrates an identical 25.0 cm³ sample of HA to which 50.0 cm³ of distilled water has been added. How does the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point compare with the first titration, and why?

options.text: It increases, because the flask now holds a larger volume of solution
It is unchanged, because the moles of HA in the flask are unchanged
It decreases, because the HA in the flask is now more dilute
It is unchanged, because adding water does not alter the pH

questions.explanation: Water changes the volume and concentration in the flask, not the moles of HA. The same moles of NaOH, so the same volume, are needed.

questions.stem: 10.0 cm³ of vinegar is diluted to 100.0 cm³ in a volumetric flask. A 25.0 cm³ portion needs 20.75 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COONa + H₂O. What was the concentration of ethanoic acid in the original vinegar, in mol dm⁻³?
questions.explanation: n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.02075 = 2.075 × 10⁻³ mol = n(acid) in the portion. 2.075 × 10⁻³ ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0830 diluted; × 10 = 0.830 in the vinegar.

questions.stem: Solution X is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq). Solution Y is 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: NH₃ is the stronger base, as solution Y is more concentrated.
NH₃ is not a base, as its formula contains no OH group.
KOH is the stronger base, as it is fully dissociated.
Both are strong bases, as both release OH⁻ ions in water.

questions.explanation: Strength is the extent of dissociation, not concentration. KOH is fully dissociated even when dilute; NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left.

questions.stem: Methyl orange can be written HInd(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + Ind⁻(aq), with HInd red and Ind⁻ yellow. A few drops are added to aqueous ammonia: the solution is yellow. Hydrochloric acid is run in. Near the end it turns orange, then red. Why?

options.text: Added H⁺ shifts the indicator equilibrium to the right, so the red Ind⁻ form builds up.
Once the ammonia is used up, added H⁺ shifts the equilibrium left, so red HInd builds up.
The indicator reacts with the ammonium chloride formed, making a red salt.
The solution turns red at exactly pH 7, when the ammonia is neutralised.

questions.explanation: While NH₃ remains, it mops up the H⁺. Past equivalence [H⁺] jumps, the pH falls through methyl orange's range, and [HInd]/[Ind⁻] = [H⁺]/Ka becomes large.

questions.stem: Vinegar (ethanoic acid, a weak acid) is in the conical flask. Sodium hydroxide is added from the burette. Which indicator should be used, and what is the colour change at the end point?

options.text: Methyl orange, from red to yellow
Either indicator, because the acid and alkali react in a 1 : 1 ratio
Phenolphthalein, from colourless to pink
Phenolphthalein, from pink to colourless

questions.explanation: Weak acid + strong base: phenolphthalein. It is colourless in the acid and turns pink when a slight excess of alkali is present.

questions.stem: In a back titration, an insoluble carbonate is added to excess hydrochloric acid, and the leftover acid is titrated with sodium hydroxide. Which amount equals the moles of HCl that reacted with the carbonate?

options.text: The moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid
The moles of HCl added to the solid at the very start
The moles of HCl added minus the moles of NaOH used in the titre
Half the moles of NaOH used in the titration of the leftover acid

questions.explanation: HCl reacts 1 : 1 with NaOH, so n(NaOH) = acid left over. Subtract it from the acid added to get the acid the carbonate used.

questions.stem: Which statement about solutions P and Q is correct? P is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq). Q is 0.50 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq), measured pH 2.53.

options.text: P has the lower pH, as a strong acid always has a lower pH than a weak one.
P has the higher pH, even though HCl is the stronger acid.
CH₃COOH must be a strong acid, as Q has a lower pH than P.
HCl is a weak acid in P, as its concentration is low.

questions.explanation: P: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.30. Only about 1 in 170 CH₃COOH molecules in Q dissociates, but Q is 1000 times more concentrated, so [H⁺] ≈ 2.95 × 10⁻³, pH 2.53. pH depends on concentration as well as strength.

questions.stem: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ ammonia is titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid. Which indicator is the most suitable? Ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4; phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0; thymol blue 8.0–9.6; alizarin yellow 10.1–12.0.

options.text: phenolphthalein
methyl orange
thymol blue
alizarin yellow

questions.explanation: Strong acid + weak base: NH₄⁺ makes the equivalence point acidic (about pH 5.3), and the steep section runs down to about pH 3.5. Methyl orange changes there.

questions.stem: A student records these titres: 24.30 cm³ (rough), 23.85 cm³, 23.40 cm³ and 23.50 cm³. Which mean titre should be used in the calculation?
questions.explanation: Only 23.40 and 23.50 cm³ are concordant (within 0.10 cm³). Their mean is 23.45 cm³.

questions.stem: An impure sample of magnesium oxide, an insoluble base, is analysed by back titration. MgO(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Assume the impurities do not react with acid. 0.400 g of the sample is added to 25.0 cm³ of 1.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl (excess). The leftover acid needs 14.30 cm³ of 0.500 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. What is the percentage by mass of MgO in the sample? (Aᵣ: O 16.0, Mg 24.3)
